    Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam 10.63.1

    ↗

    Important Words
    • aniruddham — Aniruddha
      The grandson of Kṛṣṇa, fourth member of the catur-vyūha (Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha) in Pāñcarātra theology. Gauḍīyas read the Aniruddha-Ūṣā episode as Bhagavān recovering His own kin from the realm of an asura-bhakta of Śiva.
    • bandhūnām — of the relatives
      Genitive plural of bandhu (kinsman). The Yadu clan are not just neighbors but Kṛṣṇa's own sambandhi — the verse turns on the special anguish of those who share blood with the missing devotee.
    • vārṣikaḥ — of the rainy season
      Adjective from varṣa (rain). Cāturmāsya: four months when motion is suspended, traditionally devoted to extra vrata and bhajana. Viśvanātha and Jīva Gosvāmī note this places the rescue in Mārgaśīrṣa — Kṛṣṇa's own month (Gītā 10.35).
    • anuśocatām — who were lamenting
      Present participle of anu-√śuc — sustained, sequential grieving. The same root that names the first word of the Bhagavad-gītā's first verse; Gauḍīyas hear the echo of viraha-bhāva that opens every Vaiṣṇava recovery.
    Śukadeva Gosvāmī said: O descendant of Bharata, the relatives of Aniruddha, not seeing Him return, continued to lament as the four rainy months passed.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Śukadeva Gosvāmī said: O descendant of Bharata, the relatives of Aniruddha, not seeing Him return, continued to lament as the four rainy months passed.
    Commentary

    In the sixty third chapter, Krsna defeats Jvara and Rudra, is praised by them, then cuts off the arms of Banasura, and returns to Dvaraka with Aniruddha. Starting from the month of Jyestha, Aniruddha disappeared for six months. Even the four months of the monsoon season passed and he had not returned.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The word ca means “but.” This indicates a change of subject. All the Yadus (bandhūnām) and their male and female servants (indicated by second ca) continually lamented (anu—śocatām). Four months of the monsoon completely passed (vi—atīyuh). This means it was now Mārgaśīrṣa (December). After Ūsā’s dream which occurred on the Dvādaśī during waxing phase of Vaiśākha month, Aniruddha was brought to her on the first days of Jyeṣṭha month, according to Citralekhā’s words in Hari-vaṁśa. Sapta-rātreṇa te bhīru darśayiṣyāmy ahaṁ priyam: I will show you your beloved in seven nights time. Six months passed, including even the four months of the monsoon. The first ca can also mean “and the four months of the monsoon passed.” Thus the Yadus began to worry more. O best of the Bharata clan! You were born in the Pāṇḍava family. You know that the pastimes of the Lord do not go in vain.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The word ca means “but.” This indicates a change of subject. All the Yadus (bandhūnām) and their male and female servants (indicated by second ca) continually lamented (anu—śocatām). Four months of the monsoon completely passed (vi—atīyuh). This means it was now Mārgaśīrṣa (December). After Ūsā’s dream which occurred on the Dvādaśī during waxing phase of Vaiśākha month, Aniruddha was brought to her on the first days of Jyeṣṭha month, according to Citralekhā’s words in Hari-vaṁśa. Sapta-rātreṇa te bhīru darśayiṣyāmy ahaṁ priyam: I will show you your beloved in seven nights time. Six months passed, including even the four months of the monsoon, since it was not possible to fight during the monsoon period. Or by the will of the Lord, delay was created for the battle between Bāṇa and Aniruddha. The first ca can also mean “and though the four months of the monsoon passed.” Or according to Śukadeva the abduction took place at the beginning of the monsoon. Śukadeva addresses Parīkṣit with amazement, since in spite of the presence of the Lord, the Yadus did not know the whereabouts of Aniruddha. Or it is similar to their activities while being seemingly ignorant of Abhimanyu’ fall, during the Kurukṣetra war.

    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    Like Yaśodā counting Kṛṣṇa's footsteps when He is late from the pasture, Aniruddha's relatives count the rainy months one by one. Separation from a beloved Vaiṣṇava sets a different clock — each missed day weighs as much as the one before.

    Important Words
    • nāradāt — from Nārada
      Ablative — the news comes from the parama-vaiṣṇava ṛṣi. The Bhāgavatam's own narrator-of-narrators; in Gauḍīya lineage, the dīkṣā-guru of Vyāsa and a founding link in the Brahma-Madhva-Gauḍīya paramparā.
    • kṛṣṇa-daivatāḥ — having Kṛṣṇa as their personal Deity
      Compound: kṛṣṇa + daivatāḥ (those whose iṣṭa-deva). The Yadus' identity is given here as ananya-bhakti — Kṛṣṇa is not their kinsman first and Lord second; He is their Lord first. The verse models sambandha-jñāna for the household devotee.
    • śoṇita-puram — to Śoṇitapura
      'Blood-city' — Bāṇāsura's capital. The toponym already carries the rasa: Kṛṣṇa enters a city named for blood to recover His own grandson, prefiguring the cutting of Bāṇa's thousand arms.
    • vṛṣṇayaḥ — the Vṛṣṇis
      Kṛṣṇa's own clan. The Vṛṣṇis are the human household into which Bhagavān has descended; their lament moves Him because the Lord, having accepted nara-līlā, accepts also the bonds and obligations of family.
    After hearing from Nārada the news of Aniruddha’s deeds and His capture, the Vṛṣṇis, who worshiped Lord Kṛṣṇa as their personal Deity, went to Śoṇitapura.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    After hearing from Nārada the news of Aniruddha's deeds and His capture, the Vṛṣṇis, who worshiped Lord Kṛṣṇa as their personal Deity, went to Śoṇitapura.
    Commentary

    Hearing news of Anriuddha and his activities, the Vrsnis went to Sonitapura.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Tad refers to Aniruddha. Properly it should be tasya but for metrical reasons it is tad. They heard closely, secretly the news (upa—karṇya). They went to Śonita-pura with great zeal (pra--yayuh). Kṛṣṇa was Aniruddha’s grandfather and Svayam Bhagavān. He was the most worshippable by the Yadus (kṛṣṇa-daivatāḥ). This means that they did not have fear. This also means that Kṛṣṇa went, since they followed him.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Then (tat) hearing (ākarṇya) the news about Aniruddha (tat) from Nārada, closely, secretly (upa) the Yadus went with great zeal (pra) to Śonitapura because their deity was the supreme Lord Kṛṣṇa. Since they went by his order or by his mercy, they possessed all powers.

    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    When a watchman finally names the dungeon, the rescue can begin. Nārada speaks the name 'Śoṇitapura' and the Yadus, who already worship Kṛṣṇa as their iṣṭa-devatā, simply move where their Lord is going.

    Stories
    Nārada the seed-sower

    Throughout the Bhāgavatam, Nārada appears at the precise moment a līlā needs to advance — he carries word of Prahlāda to Hiraṇyakaśipu, of Dhruva's tapas to the Lord, of Ajāmila's son's name to the messengers. Here he carries word of Aniruddha's capture to Dvārakā.

    Gauḍīyas read Nārada-muni as the eternal traveling preceptor: he never holds information for himself; every word he carries plants a seed of bhakti-līlā in another field.

    Important Words
    • rāma-kṛṣṇa-anuvartinaḥ — following Balarāma and Kṛṣṇa
      Compound: rāma + kṛṣṇa + anuvartinaḥ (those who follow after). The Sātvatas are defined by anuvṛtti — following, not leading. Bhakti's grammar: the devotee's place is behind the Lord, never in front.
    • sātvata-ṛṣabhāḥ — the bulls of the Sātvata clan
      Compound: sātvata (the devotee clan, from sat-vat, 'possessing truth') + ṛṣabha (bull, chief). The Sātvatas are the prototype of the bhakta-vaṁśa; Gauḍīyas trace their own sampradāya's name 'Bhāgavata' to this same root-cluster.
    • akṣauhiṇībhiḥ dvādaśabhiḥ — with twelve military divisions
      An akṣauhiṇī is a complete fourfold army (Mahābhārata's standard unit). Twelve here equals the Pāṇḍava-Kaurava combined strength at Kurukṣetra — the verse signals that recovering one bhakta's grandson is treated with the gravity of cosmic war.
    • rurudhuḥ — they besieged
      Perfect plural of √rudh (to obstruct, surround). The same verb-field as nirodha (restraint). Bhagavān's army puts an asura's city under the kind of nirodha that bhakti puts on the wayward senses.
    With Lord Balarāma and Lord Kṛṣṇa in the lead, the chiefs of the Sātvata clan — Pradyumna, Sātyaki, Gada, Sāmba, Sāraṇa, Nanda, Upananda, Bhadra and others — converged with an army of twelve divisions and laid siege to Bāṇasura’s capital, completely surrounding the city on all sides.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    With Lord Balarāma and Lord Kṛṣṇa in the lead, the chiefs of the Sātvata clan—Pradyumna, Sātyaki, Gada, Sāmba, Sāraṇa, Nanda, Upananda, Bhadra and others—converged with an army of twelve divisions and laid siege to Bāṇasura's capital, completely surrounding the city on all sides.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The word atha indicates that they all followed after Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma. Nanda, Upananda and Bhadra were members of the Yadu dynasty. They brought their troops together out of affection (sam--etāḥ) and surrounded the city completely (samantāt).

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Atha means even Śāraṇa, who was well known for bravery. Or this means “after Sāmba” showing the order of the warriors following after Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma. Nanda, Upananda and Bhadra were members of the Yadu dynasty. Other warriors like Kṛtavarmā are included. Or Nanda, Upananda, and Bhadrasena, and others such as Śrīdāmā (ādyāḥ), refer to the leaders of the cowherd troops who lived in Dvārakā out of affection for Kṛṣṇa, or who went to battle with the Yadus often. Or they came from Vraja at this time quickly out of affection, worried about a battle with Śiva. The word atha can mean this. They followed in front of Pradyumna and the rest. Balarāma is mentioned before Kṛṣṇa because he was the elder brother. Or out of affection he went in front during battle. Balarāma (rāma) gave pleasure to all and Kṛṣṇa attracted everyone because of his affection. The troops gathered with affection (sametāḥ) and continually attacked the fortress because they were the best of the Yadus. Or because of the presence of the cowherds they were the best according to the example of the umbrella carriers go (said if one person, the king, has an umbrella, everyone is said to have an umbrella). Or the cowherds were also Yadus according to Skanda Purānā. Or the Yadus were the best of devotees (sātvata).

    Personal Guidance
    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    When the head of a household goes to recover a stolen child, every brother and son walks behind him. Balarāma and Kṛṣṇa take the lead, and Pradyumna, Sātyaki, Sāmba and the rest follow — twelve akṣauhiṇīs of a single family arrayed in one ring around Bāṇa's gates.

    Stories
    Rāma's army at Laṅkā

    The Rāmāyaṇa pattern returns here: an avatāra goes to recover a stolen kinsperson, and the loyal host follows. There Hanumān and the vānaras encircle Laṅkā; here Pradyumna and the Sātvatas encircle Śoṇitapura.

    Gauḍīyas read the parallel as deliberate — the Bhāgavatam consistently mirrors Rāma-līlā inside Kṛṣṇa-līlā to show one Bhagavān across descents, with bhakti as the common army.

    Important Words
    • prākāra — ramparts
      The defensive wall around a fortified city. Gauḍīya commentators read the asura's prākāra as the outer shell of false security the conditioned soul builds against Bhagavān — the very thing that must fall before śaraṇāgati can begin.
    • ruṣā-āviṣṭaḥ — filled with anger
      Compound participle: ruṣā (with rage) + āviṣṭa (entered, possessed). Anger does not arise in Bāṇa; it enters him — the asura is occupied by his own krodha as a deity occupies a temple. The Gītā's diagnosis (2.62–63) made flesh.
    • abhiniryayau — he went out
      Aorist of abhi + nis + √yā (to march out against). Bāṇa's mistake is to come out: as long as he stayed inside the city of his own pride, the wall sheltered him; the moment he steps out to meet Bhagavān as an equal, the loss has already been recorded.
    • tulya-sainyaḥ — with an equal-sized army
      Compound: tulya (equal) + sainya (army). The asura's calculus is parity — twelve akṣauhiṇīs to twelve. Bhagavān will not be matched by counting; the verse sets up the lesson that numerical equality means nothing against the wielder of Śārṅga.
    Bāṇāsura became filled with anger upon seeing them destroy his city’s suburban gardens, ramparts, watchtowers and gateways, and thus he went out to confront them with an army of equal size.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Bāṇāsura became filled with anger upon seeing them destroy his city's suburban gardens, ramparts, watchtowers and gateways, and thus he went out to confront them with an army of equal size.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Seeing astutely (while counting the enemy troops) his gardens being destroyed, he went out facing they (abhi—niryayau), with an equal number of troops. He had more troops, but to show he would fight justly out of great pride, he brought only the same number of troops to fight.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    They destroyed progressively interior areas of the city or more excellent elements of the city. Seeing this directly and through spies, Bāṇa left the city to face them with an equal army of twelve akṣauhiṇīs since he had a great number of troops. He had more troops, but to show he would fight justly out of great pride, he brought only the same number of troops to fight.

    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    An asura's pride is built like a city wall — gardens, ramparts, watchtowers, gateways, each course of stone a fortification of false ego. When Kṛṣṇa's army cracks one stone, the demon roars; Bāṇa's anger here is the sound of ahaṅkāra being demolished from outside.

    Important Words
    • bhagavān rudraḥ — Lord Rudra
      Rudra is given the epithet bhagavān — a designation reserved for those possessing the six opulences. Gauḍīyas read this carefully: Śiva is a śaktyāveśa-avatāra and the topmost Vaiṣṇava, deserving of bhagavān, yet always subordinate to Kṛṣṇa as the chapter's stuti will confirm.
    • nandi-vṛṣabham — the bull Nandi
      Compound: nandi (the joyful one) + vṛṣabha (bull). Śiva's vāhana, dharma personified as bull. He rides his own carrier of dharma into a battle that dharma itself will end by surrendering to Kṛṣṇa.
    • sa-sutaḥ — with his son
      Compound: sa (with) + sutaḥ (son), i.e. Kārtikeya/Skanda. The family of Kailāsa moves as one, the way the family of Dvārakā moves as one — two households of devotion meet on the same field.
    • pramathaiḥ — with the Pramathas
      Śiva's intimate gaṇa — fierce attendants. The verse stages a confrontation of associates: Śiva's pramathas versus Kṛṣṇa's Sātvatas, the comparison itself instructing on the difference between aiśvarya-bhakti and śuddha-bhakti.
    Lord Rudra, accompanied by his son Kārtikeya and the Pramathas, came riding on Nandi, his bull carrier, to fight Balarāma and Kṛṣṇa on Bāṇa’s behalf.
    Purport

    Śrīla Śrīdhara Svāmī states that the word bhagavān is used here to indicate that Lord Śiva is by nature all-knowing and thus well aware of Lord Kṛṣṇa’s greatness. Still, although Śiva knew Lord Kṛṣṇa would defeat him, he joined the battle against Him to demonstrate the glories of the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Śrīla Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura states that Lord Śiva entered the battle for two reasons: first, to increase Lord Kṛṣṇa’s pleasure and enthusiasm; and second, to demonstrate that the Lord’s incarnation as Kṛṣṇa, although enacting humanlike pastimes, is superior to other avatāras, such as Lord Rāmacandra. Śrīla Viśvanātha Cakravartī further states in this regard that Yoga-māyā, Lord Kṛṣṇa’s internal potency, bewildered Lord Śiva just as she had bewildered Brahmā. In support of this statement, the ācārya cites the phrase brahma-rudrādi-mohanam from Bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhu. Of course, Yoga-māyā’s job is to make fine arrangements for the Lord’s pastimes, and thus Śiva became enthusiastic to battle the Supreme Lord, Kṛṣṇa.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Lord Rudra, accompanied by his son Kārtikeya and the Pramathas, came riding on Nandi, his bull carrier, to fight Balarāma and Kṛṣṇa on Bāṇa's behalf.
    Commentary

    Rudra fought on behalf of Banasura just to show Banasura his faults by making him experience suffering. He is addressed as bhagavan to indicate that he was omniscient, and thus he fought to show the greatness of Krsna by being defeated by Krsna. This is the opinion of ancient authorities. As in the case of Brahma, Yogamaya, instructed by the lila sakti, bewildered Siva and his followers in order to give pleasure and enthusiasm of fighting to the Lord, and in order to show the supremacy and extraordinary qualities of Krsna over all other avataras including Rama, when he appeared performing human pastimes.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Śiva fought on Bāṇa’s behalf to show Bāṇa’s fault of bad association. Another version has bāṇārtham. Śiva, being omniscient (bhagavān), knew Kṛṣṇa’s powers. He fought to show to Bāṇa and others Kṛṣṇa’s powers by his own defeat.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Śiva had affection for his devotee (bhagavān). Thus he drives away (dra) suffering (rud) of his devotees Thus he fought with Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma. Otherwise they would be displeased with him as a devotee.

    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    A guru who has accepted a vow to protect a disciple will appear at the doorway of any battle that disciple has entered — even one he should not have started. Rudra rides Nandi to Śoṇitapura not because Bāṇa is right, but because Bāṇa is his.

    Stories
    Śiva's vow to Bāṇa

    The Bhāgavatam (10.62) records that Bāṇa, by long worship and dance before Śiva, secured the boon that Śiva himself would guard his city. The vow binds Rudra to ride out today against Kṛṣṇa.

    Gauḍīyas read this as the great Vaiṣṇava paradox: Śiva, the topmost vaiṣṇava (vaiṣṇavānāṁ yathā śambhuḥ, SB 12.13.16), is bound by his own promise to fight Viṣṇu's own descent. The chapter exists to resolve that knot through stuti.

    Important Words
    • kṛṣṇa-śaṅkarayoḥ — of Kṛṣṇa and Śaṅkara
      Dual genitive. Gauḍīya commentators (Jīva, Viśvanātha) consistently read this dual as the doctrinal anchor of the chapter: the two are paired in narrative, but the stuti to come (vv. 34–44) will resolve the pairing as servant-and-served, not peer-and-peer.
    • adbhutam — wonderful, astonishing
      From √abhū (to come to be, beyond ordinary becoming). The battle is adbhuta-rasa: marvel arises because both combatants are loved by the spectator, and the spectator (Brahmā and company, v. 9) is waiting to see which way the line of subordination will resolve.
    • roma-harṣaṇam — hair-raising
      Compound: roman (body hair) + harṣaṇa (causing to stand on end). The same bodily sign Gauḍīyas count among the eight sāttvika-bhāvas — what the verse names as the audience's thrill is also the somatic signature of bhāva-bhakti.
    • pradyumna-guhayoḥ — of Pradyumna and Kārtikeya (Guha)
      Dual genitive. Pradyumna — Kāma reborn as Kṛṣṇa's son — meets Guha, Skanda. Gauḍīyas note: the Lord's own sons fight the demigods' sons; the upper layer of the war mirrors the lower layer.
    A most astonishing, tumultuous and hair-raising battle then commenced, with Lord Kṛṣṇa matched against Lord Śaṅkara, and Pradyumna against Kārtikeya.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The fighting was very congested (su-tumulam), astonishing and hair-raising. Even hearing about it would make the hairs stand on end. First a general description of the pairs of combatants is listed. Details of the fight are given later.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    There was great confusion (sutumulam), most astonishing or extraordinary. It made hairs stand on end. After the general description details are given. Śukadeva expresses astonishment at the battle, or the battle between Kṛṣṇa and Śiva. O king! Or the conflict was effulgent (rājan).

    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    When the sun and the moon stand opposite in the same sky, neither is diminished — both shine and one bows to the other in season. Kṛṣṇa and Śaṅkara meeting bow-to-trident is exactly this kind of cosmic alignment, not a contest of equals.

    • balena saha — with Balarāma
      Bala — strength itself personified. Gauḍīyas read Balarāma as ādi-guru, the first expansion of Kṛṣṇa as Saṅkarṣaṇa; here He confronts the asura ministers because the guru-tattva is what dismantles the asura-vṛtti.
    • kumbhāṇḍa-kūpakarṇābhyām — with Kumbhāṇḍa and Kūpakarṇa
      Bāṇa's ministers — pot-belly and pit-ears. The Bhāgavatam names them with grotesque body-compounds to mark their tāmasa-quality; their bodies are the visible distortion of their inner state.
    • sāmbasya — Sāmba's
      Kṛṣṇa's son by Jāmbavatī. He fights Bāṇa's son — the lineages mirror each other. Sāmba's later story (SB 11) carries cautionary weight; here he is still in his glorious phase, fighting at his father's flank.
    • sātyakeḥ — Sātyaki's
      Yuyudhāna — Kṛṣṇa's dear sakha and disciple of Arjuna in archery. The verse pairs him with the chief asura because sakhya-bhakti is the rasa that does not flinch from confrontation on the Lord's behalf.

    Commentary

    Balarāma was paired with Kumbhāṇda and Kūpakarṇa.

    Analogy

      Compound: brahmā + ādayaḥ (and so on). Brahmā heads the list of celestial spectators — appropriate, since vv. 35–36 of this chapter will name him as Bhagavān's dhiṣaṇā (intelligence). The grandfather of the universe attends to learn the grammar of subordination.
    • siddha-cāraṇāḥ — Siddhas and Cāraṇas
      Compound: siddha (perfected beings, masters of mystic siddhi) + cāraṇa (celestial bards). Gauḍīyas note that even those who have attained the eightfold siddhis come merely to watch — siddhi is for spectating; bhakti is for participating.
    • vimānaiḥ — in celestial airplanes
      Instrumental plural of vimāna. The vimāna is the standard Purāṇic vehicle of devas; the verse stresses that this battle is staged for the upper realms to witness, not concealed — Bhagavān's victories are public theology.
    • draṣṭum — to see
      Infinitive of √dṛś. Darśana — the same word that names the goal of every Vaiṣṇava pilgrimage. Bhagavān always provides darśana, even in the form of a battlefield; the upper worlds know this and come for it.
    Brahmā and the other ruling demigods, along with Siddhas, Cāraṇas and great sages, as well as Gandharvas, Apsarās and Yakṣas, all came in their celestial airplanes to watch.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Brahmā and the other ruling demigods, along with Siddhas, Cāraṇas and great sages, as well as Gandharvas, Apsarās and Yakṣas, all came in their celestial airplanes to watch.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Brahmā is mentioned first since he was the head of the devatās. The list is from greater to lesser beings.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The list of those who observed is from superior to inferior. The devatās came mainly to make Śiva come to his senses.

    Analogy

    When two great kings prepare to meet on a field, every wise man in the kingdom postpones business to watch. Brahmā, the sages, the Siddhas — the heavens empty into airplanes because the question being settled below is not 'who will win' but 'what is the order of the worlds'.

    Important Words
    • śaṅkara-anucarān — the followers of Śaṅkara
      Compound: śaṅkara + anucara (one who follows after). The same anucara-pattern that names the Vaiṣṇava's place behind Kṛṣṇa — here applied to Śiva's gaṇa. Gauḍīyas note the parallel: every personality has His own train, but the trains themselves are subordinate.
    • śauriḥ — Kṛṣṇa, descendant of Śūra
      From Śūra, Kṛṣṇa's paternal grandfather (and Vasudeva's father). The patronymic anchors Bhagavān in the Yadu kula even as He acts cosmically — Gauḍīyas prize this constant grounding of the universal in the household.
    • bhūta-pramatha — Bhūtas and Pramathas
      Compound: bhūta (ghostly beings) + pramatha (Śiva's churning attendants). The tāmasa fringe of Śiva's retinue — appropriate to him as Lord of cremation grounds, but not equipped to face the wielder of Śārṅga.
    • śārṅga-dhanuḥ-cyutaiḥ — discharged from the bow Śārṅga
      Compound: śārṅga (made of horn) + dhanu (bow) + cyuta (fallen from, released). Kṛṣṇa's own bow, paired with Sudarśana and Pāñcajanya among His personal weapons. Each arrow carries the will of Bhagavān, not the malice of a warrior.
    With sharp-pointed arrows discharged from His bow Śārṅga, Lord Kṛṣṇa drove away the various followers of Lord Śiva — Bhūtas, Pramathas, Guhyakas, Ḍākinīs, Yātudhānas, Vetālas, Vināyakas, Pretas, Mātās, Piśācas, Kuṣmāṇḍas and Brahma-rākṣasas.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    With sharp-pointed arrows discharged from His bow Śārṅga, Lord Kṛṣṇa drove away the various followers of Lord Śiva—Bhūtas, Pramathas, Guhyakas, Ḍākinīs, Yātudhānas, Vetālas, Vināyakas, Pretas, Mātās, Piśācas, Kuṣmāṇḍas and Brahma-rākṣasas.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Another version has bhūta-mātṛ-piśācān. But this would be repetition since bhūta-pramatha-guhyakān is found in the previous verse. The mothers of the bhūtas are persons other than the Pārvatī and mothers of the devatās. Kṛṣṇa drove them away with arrows shot from the Sārṅga bow, but did not kill them since they were the followers of his devotee Śiva. This shows his great mercy.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Kṛṣṇa defeated the follows dispatched by Śiva, in his fight with Kṛṣṇa. This is described in two verses. The Bhūtas were born from devatās. This list is progressively more ferocious and inferior in nature. Pretas are a type of Piśāca. Kṛṣṇa drove them away, using arrows shot from his bow. Het did not kill them because they were followers of Śiva. The arrows were thus unfailing in their target and swift.

    Analogy

    Like a strong wind that scatters fog without injuring the field beneath, Kṛṣṇa's Śārṅga-arrows do not crush Śiva's followers — they merely drive them away. The Lord clears a path to His real interlocutor; the supporting host is dispersed, not destroyed.

    Important Words
    • piṇākī — the wielder of Pināka
      Śiva's epithet — Pināka is his bow. The verse names him by his weapon to parallel Kṛṣṇa as Śārṅga-pāṇi; the two are framed as bow-wielders, equals in posture, unequal in metaphysical rank.
    • śārṅga-pāṇiḥ — the bearer of Śārṅga in His hand
      Compound: śārṅga + pāṇi (hand). One of Viṣṇu's standard epithets; the hand-and-weapon-compound (cakra-pāṇi, padma-pāṇi, śaṅkha-pāṇi) marks the deity by what He holds. Bhagavān is identified by what He carries for His devotees' sake.
    • prati-astraiḥ — with counter-weapons
      Compound: prati (against, in reply) + astra (weapon). The verb-field of bhakti's response-grammar: every śakti has its corresponding counter; Bhagavān's hand is always already holding the answer.
    • avismitaḥ — not at all astonished
      Compound: a (not) + vi-smita (astonished). Śiva's astras astonish the worlds; they do not astonish their source. Gauḍīyas read this as the precise sign of Bhagavān-tattva: He is the one for whom nothing else is wonderful.
    Lord Śiva, wielder of the trident, shot various weapons at Lord Kṛṣṇa, wielder of Śārṅga. But Lord Kṛṣṇa was not in the least perplexed: He neutralized all these weapons with appropriate counterweapons.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Lord Śiva, wielder of the trident, shot various weapons at Lord Kṛṣṇa, wielder of Śārṅga. But Lord Kṛṣṇa was not in the least perplexed: He neutralized all these weapons with appropriate counterweapons.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    They used weapons like the brahmāstra, shooting them separately. They both used bows, fighting according to the rules. Kṛṣṇa shot his arrows casually (avismitaḥ).

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    They used weapons like the brahmāstra, shooting them separately. Kṛṣṇa, holder of the bow, fought only with a bow rather than use his cakra because he was at a great distance from Śiva. Śiva, holder the trident, also fought with a bow. Kṛṣṇa was not proud (avismitaḥ) when Śiva used his weapons. Or he did not smile during this battle.

    Analogy

    When a master swordsman fights a student, every cut is met with its exact counter — not because the master is straining, but because he is teaching. Kṛṣṇa meets each of Śiva's astras with the appointed reply, and the lesson being taught is who is teacher and who is student.

    Important Words
    • brahma-astrasya — of the brahmāstra
      The highest mantra-weapon, invoked by brahma-mantras. Kṛṣṇa neutralizes it with another brahmāstra: same family, same potency. Gauḍīyas note that even the Veda's own most fearful astra is in His drawer.
    • pāśupatasya — of the pāśupata weapon
      Śiva's personal supreme astra — the one Arjuna received after the Kirāta encounter. Even this, the asset of asset-holders, is matched here. Kṛṣṇa's reply is nārāyaṇāstra, His own personal weapon — Viṣṇu-tattva trumps Pāśupata-tattva.
    • naijam — His own
      From nija — one's very own. Bhagavān deploys His nija-astra against Śiva's nija-astra. The chapter teaches by parallel structure: each side brings what is most personal; on the Viṣṇu side, the personal weapon is sovereign.
    • pārjanyam — the rain weapon
      From Parjanya, the rain-cloud deity. Cited in Gītā 3.14 — annād bhavanti bhūtāni, parjanyād anna-sambhavaḥ. The cosmic order of element-against-element is in Kṛṣṇa's hand even on a battlefield.
    Lord Kṛṣṇa counteracted a brahmāstra with another brahmāstra, a wind weapon with a mountain weapon, a fire weapon with a rain weapon, and Lord Śiva’s personal pāśupatāstra weapon with His own personal weapon, the nārāyaṇāstra.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Lord Kṛṣṇa counteracted a brahmāstra with another brahmāstra, a wind weapon with a mountain weapon, a fire weapon with a rain weapon, and Lord Śiva's personal pāśupatāstra weapon with His own personal weapon, the nārāyaṇāstra.
    Commentary

    Counteracting Siva’s weapons is described in this verse. Brahmastra was countered with a Brahmastra. The verb "released" is understood from the previous verse. Krsna countered the pasupata weapon with his own weapon (naijam), the Narayana astra.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    When Śiva used a brahmāstra, Kṛṣṇa also used a brahmāstra. The verb is in the previous verse. Naijam means “his own.”

    Analogy

    Fire is quenched not by argument but by rain; wind is stilled not by another wind but by mountain. So each of Śiva's weapons is met by the element appointed to receive it. Kṛṣṇa is the ledger in which every śakti's opposite is already written.

    Important Words
    • mohayitvā — having bewildered
      Causative absolutive of √muh (to be deluded). Mohana is one of Kṛṣṇa's signature actions — He bewilders Brahmā in SB 10.13, Arjuna at Gītā 11. Here even Śiva is briefly bewildered; the verse establishes the asymmetry the stuti will articulate.
    • giriśam — the lord of the mountain (Śiva)
      Compound: giri (mountain) + īśa (lord). Kailāsa's resident. The mountain-lord is given a brief lapse — Gauḍīyas read this not as Śiva's defeat but as Bhagavān's gentleness in not engaging him fully.
    • jṛmbhaṇa-astreṇa — with the yawning weapon
      Compound: jṛmbhaṇa (yawning) + astra. Even the names of Kṛṣṇa's weapons carry līlā-flavor; He could end Śiva but instead He yawns him. The form of victory is itself the proof of supremacy.
    • jaghāna — He struck down
      Perfect tense of √han (to slay). Reserved here for Bāṇa's army, not for Śiva or Bāṇa himself. The verb's distribution in the verse is theology: Bhagavān slays the army; He bewilders the deity; He will eventually spare the bhakta-asura.
    After bewildering Lord Śiva by making him yawn with a yawning weapon, Lord Kṛṣṇa proceeded to strike down Bāṇāsura’s army with His sword, club and arrows.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    After bewildering Lord Śiva by making him yawn with a yawning weapon, Lord Kṛṣṇa proceeded to strike down Bāṇāsura's army with His sword, club and arrows.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Kṛṣṇa made Śiva faint with his yawning weapon. Hari-vaṁśa says: sa-śaraḥ sa-dhanuś caiva haras tenāśu jṛmbhitaḥ | saṁjṣāṁ na lebhe bhagavān vijetāsura-rakṣasām || Śiva, still holding his arrows and bow, suddenly yawned and lost consciousness because of the Lord’s weapon. The Lord was the conqueror of the demons. The sword, the club and arrows are progressively more effective at a distance.

    Analogy

    Even a great warrior, set to yawning at the wrong moment, drops his bow. Kṛṣṇa does not defeat Śiva by force; He bewilders him for one breath with a yawning astra and turns to dispose of Bāṇa's army during the gap. Līlā, not violence.

    Important Words
    • skandaḥ — Skanda (Kārtikeya)
      From √skand (to leap, jet forth) — named for the manner of his birth from Śiva's tejas. Commander of the deva-army, lord of war. Even his retreat here is honorable: he yields to a higher power, not to a peer.
    • pradyumna-bāṇa-oghaiḥ — by the flood of Pradyumna's arrows
      Compound: pradyumna + bāṇa (arrows) + ogha (flood). The same word bāṇa names both arrows and the demon; the verse plays on this: the demon Bāṇa's domain is being struck down by Pradyumna's bāṇas (arrows).
    • śikhinā — on his peacock
      Instrumental of śikhin (one with a crest, i.e. peacock). Skanda's vāhana. The peacock, Kṛṣṇa's own ornament (mayūra-piccha), here serves the retreating son of Śiva — the symbol itself bows toward Vraja.
    • apākramat — he retreated
      Aorist of apa-√kram (to step away). Honorable withdrawal, not flight. Gauḍīyas note: Skanda's retreat is the demigod-pattern — when faced with Bhagavān's expansion, the demigod yields without dishonor.

    Kartikeya (skanda) left the battlefield with his peacock (sakhina).

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Having described Kṛṣṇa’s victory, now Śukadeva describes other victories of his followers in two verses. He fled on the peacock because without it, he could not move, being in great pain.

    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    Even Skanda, born of Śiva's tejas to slay Tāraka, retreats before Kṛṣṇa's son. Pradyumna — Kāma-deva reborn in Dvārakā — reminds the cosmos that Kṛṣṇa's family contains every śakti the demigod-family contains, in fuller measure.

    Stories
    Skanda's birth and Pradyumna's birth

    Skanda is born from Śiva's seed received by Agni and the Kṛttikās, raised to lead the deva army against Tāraka. Pradyumna is born to Kṛṣṇa and Rukmiṇī, then stolen by Śambara, recovered and raised by Māyāvatī (Rati). Each is a war-leader son of his Lord.

    The Bhāgavatam stages their meeting on this field so the question is settled in flesh: Bhagavān's son outranks the demigod's son. Gauḍīyas read this as confirming the lineage-asymmetry between Vaikuṇṭha and the upper material lokas.

    Important Words
    • muṣala-arditau — tormented by the club
      Compound: muṣala (Balarāma's club) + ardita (afflicted). The muṣala is Balarāma's signature weapon, paired with His plough (hala). Gauḍīyas read the muṣala as the implement of the ādi-guru striking down ignorance at its root.
    • petatuḥ — the two fell
      Perfect dual of √pat (to fall). The same root that gives 'patita' — fallen. The asura-generals fall in the literal sense the conditioned soul falls in the figurative; Balarāma's club ends both falls when wielded with grace.
    • hata-nāthāni — whose leaders were killed
      Compound: hata (slain) + nātha (lord, protector). The asura army's nātha is mortal; the bhakta's Nātha is eternal. The verse contrasts the two protections without naming the contrast — the reader is meant to feel it.
    • dudruvuḥ — they fled
      Perfect of √dru (to run). When the false shelter falls, the dependents scatter — the inverse picture of śaraṇāgati, where the true Shelter never falls and the surrendered never need to flee.
    Kumbhāṇḍa and Kūpakarṇa, tormented by Lord Balarāma’s club, fell down dead. When the soldiers of these two demons saw that their leaders had been killed, they scattered in all directions.

    It should be understood that Bāṇa’s son was defeated by Sāmba.

    Analogy

    A tree falls and the birds in its branches scatter. When Kumbhāṇḍa and Kūpakarṇa drop under Balarāma's club, the soldiers who had been roosting on their leadership take wing in every direction. Bhakti-grounded leadership stands; tāmasa-leadership collapses underfoot.

    Important Words
    • viśīryamāṇam — being torn apart
      Present passive participle of vi-√śṝ (to break, scatter). The army does not collapse all at once; it is being torn apart in real time. The verse marks the moment Bāṇa sees his structure dissolve.
    • ati-amarṣitaḥ — extremely intolerant
      Compound: ati (very) + amarṣita (unable to tolerate). Amarṣa is the asura's reflex — what bhakti calls titikṣā (forbearance) the asura cannot perform. Bāṇa's intolerance is the inverse of the Vaiṣṇava's chief virtue.
    • abhyadravat — rushed toward
      Imperfect of abhi-√dru (to run at). The same root as dudruvuḥ in the previous verse — his soldiers ran away, he runs toward. Both motions end in his loss; the asura cannot stay still long enough to surrender.
    • hitvā eva sātyakim — abandoning Sātyaki
      Bāṇa's mistake is to break engagement with his appointed opponent to challenge the Lord directly. Gauḍīyas read this as the conditioned soul's typical leap: skipping the guru (here, Sātyaki, who would have ended him in due course) to confront Bhagavān unprepared.
    Bāṇāsura was furious to see his entire military force being torn apart. Leaving his fight with Sātyaki, he charged across the battlefield on his chariot and attacked Lord Kṛṣṇa.

    Commentary

    Seeing his army (balam) scattered, Bāṇa left his fight with Sātyaki and attacked Kṛṣṇa.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    His troops were destroyed or broken. Or he saw in the fight with Sātyakī that his power had withered away. Fighting with him was useless. Why waste my powers? I should fight with the main opponent, Kṛṣṇa. He thus charged towards Kṛṣṇa quickly since he mounted a chariot with a charioteer named Nandīśvara. nandīśa-saṁgṛhītāśvam adhirūḍho mahāratham / bāṇas tatrāyayau yoddhuṁ kṛṣṇa-kārṣṇibalaiḥ saha // Bāṇa, mounted on a huge chariot with horses guided by Nandīśa, then came to fight with Kṛṣṇa and his armies. Viṣṇu Purāṇa Though it was not proper to give up fighting the opponent, he gave up Sātyaki without winning (eva has meaning of vā) because he was very angry.

    Analogy

    An asura's logic is escalation: when the periphery breaks, charge the center. Bāṇa abandons Sātyaki and rushes Kṛṣṇa — exactly the wrong direction, the way a moth charges the very flame that is already consuming its kin.

    • yugapat — simultaneously
      Adverb — at one and the same time. Bāṇa's pride is in the simultaneity; verse 19 will reuse the same word against him when Kṛṣṇa cuts all his bows yugapat. Bhagavān answers simultaneity with simultaneity.
    • śarau dvau dvau — two arrows each
      Distributive: two-two on each string. The repetition stages the asura's frantic doubling; Bhagavān's reply will be a single Sudarśana. One cakra against a thousand bows is the lesson of bhakti's economy.
    • raṇa-durmadaḥ — intoxicated by battle
      Compound: raṇa (battle) + durmada (badly intoxicated). Mada — pride and intoxication together — is one of the six enemies (kāma, krodha, lobha, moha, mada, mātsarya). Bāṇa is its perfect specimen, intoxicated on the very combat that is about to end him.

    Important Words
    • ciccheda — He cut
      Perfect of √chid (to cut, split). Will recur in verse 32 when Bāṇa's own arms are cut. The verb carries the chapter's tactile signature: Bhagavān is the cutter of false structures, from bow-strings to arms to ahaṅkāra itself.
    • śaṅkham apūrayat — He sounded His conchshell
      Pāñcajanya, blown by Kṛṣṇa at every decisive turn in Mahābhārata and Bhāgavatam. The conch is the auditory mūrti of Bhagavān's voice; its sound is meant to be heard by the relatives back in Dvārakā as much as by the asura on the field.
    • yugapat — simultaneously
      The same yugapat Bāṇa used in v. 18 to boast of his simultaneous draw is now used against him. The verse's grammar is the chapter's verdict: whatever the asura claims to do all-at-once, Bhagavān undoes all-at-once.
    • sārathim ratham aśvān ca hatvā — having struck down driver, chariot and horses
      The serial list strips Bāṇa of his three supports in succession. Gauḍīyas note: chariot, driver, horses correspond to body, intellect, senses (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.3.3) — Bhagavān is dismantling the asura at every layer of the self before sparing the core.

    Lord Śrī Hari split every one of Bāṇāsura's bows simultaneously, and also struck down his chariot driver, chariot and horses. The Lord then sounded His conchshell.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Bāṇa’s bows broke simultaneously on contact with Kṛṣṇa’s arrows. This was Kṛṣṇa’s pastime since he was endowed with all powers (bhagavān). He then destroyed the charioteers, chariots and horses. Thus he was called Hari, one who destroys (saṁharati).

    Important Words
    • koṭarā nāma — named Koṭarā
      Koṭarā — literally 'hollow of a tree'. Bāṇa's mother. The Bhāgavatam names her by a hollow because her stratagem is to create a hollow in Bhagavān's gaze, a momentary inattention through which her son can escape.
    • nagnā — naked
      The desperate maternal weapon — Koṭarā weaponizes her own body's exposure to compel Kṛṣṇa's modesty. Gauḍīyas read this as proof that Bhagavān, having accepted nara-līlā, accepts also its proprieties; He could see through it but chooses to honor them.
    • putra-prāṇa-rirakṣayā — with the desire to protect her son's life
      Compound: putra (son) + prāṇa (life) + rirakṣayā (with intent to protect). Maternal vātsalya in the asura register — even on this side of the line, a mother's wish to save her son moves the cosmos. The Lord will honor that wish in the larger frame by sparing Bāṇa entirely (v. 47).
    • avatasthe — she stood before
      Perfect of ava-√sthā (to stand near, present oneself). The same root that gives sthāyī-bhāva — standing-emotion. Koṭarā's standing forces a counter-standing from Bhagavān: He averts His face. Bhakti's grammar acknowledges even an opponent's standing.
    Just then Bāṇāsura’s mother, Koṭarā, desiring to save her son’s life, appeared before Lord Kṛṣṇa naked and with her hair undone.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Just then Bāṇāsura's mother, Koṭarā, desiring to save her son's life, appeared before Lord Kṛṣṇa naked and with her hair undone.
    Commentary

    Bana's mother, named Kothara, sometimes called Kotari, is a form of Parvati worshipped by the demons. With a desire to protect her son (riraksaya), she appeared naked.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    According to Hari-vaṁśa, Bāṇa became Śiva’ṣ son by great austerities. Because the mother was thus considered to be like Pārvatī she was called Koṭarā, another form of Pārvatī. In Hari-vaṁśa she is famous as Koṭarī. Śiva says, “Please save him, O Pārvatī. Go quickly to save Bāṇa without delay.” kṛṣṇasyaikasya tad rūpaṁ darśayat pārśvam āgatā antardhānam upāgamya tyaktvā sā vāsasī punaḥ / paritrāṇāya bāṇasya vijayādhiṣṭhitā tataḥ / pramukhe vāsudevasya digvāsāḥ koṭavī sthitā // She came close to Kṛṣṇa in her form. Giving up invisibility, she appeared before him while wearing clothing. In order to protect Bāṇa she then stood there facing Kṛṣṇa, without clothing. Koṭarī is another name of Bāṇa’s mother. According to Viṣṇu Purāṇa however Koṭarī is the name of devatā of the demons who possessed powerful mantras. Nāmnā daiteya-vidyābhūt koḍarī purato hareḥ: Koṭarī, who had demonic knowledge, appeared before Kṛṣṇa. She is also called Kotavī. Another version has rirakṣiṣayā instead of rīraakṣayā.

    Important Words
    • tiryak-mukhaḥ — with face turned aside
      Compound: tiryak (sideways, obliquely) + mukha (face). The Bhāgavatam's iconography of Bhagavān's chastity. Gauḍīyas read this gesture as Kṛṣṇa's natural ācāra; the master of the gopīs' rasa is also the model of dṛṣṭi-saṁyama.
    • gadāgrajaḥ — the elder brother of Gada
      Compound: gada (Kṛṣṇa's younger brother by Rohiṇī's co-wife Devakī's sister) + agraja (elder). A relational name. Even in the climax of cosmic battle, the Bhāgavatam reaches for a household epithet — bhakti always remembers family.
    • chinna-dhanvā — with broken bow
      Compound: chinna (cut) + dhanu (bow). Bāṇa is now without his characteristic weapon — and yet still called 'Bāṇa' (arrow). The verse's irony: he carries the name of the weapon he no longer possesses.
    • āviśat puram — entered the city
      Aorist of ā-√viś (to enter). The same root as āveśa. Bāṇa retreats into his city — the temporary shelter — when his real, permanent shelter (Bhagavān's mercy) is one verse away from being granted through Śiva's stuti.
    Lord Gadāgraja turned His face away to avoid seeing the naked woman, and Bāṇāsura — deprived of his chariot, his bow shattered — took the opportunity to flee into his city.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Lord Gadāgraja turned His face away to avoid seeing the naked woman, and Bāṇāsura—deprived of his chariot, his bow shattered—took the opportunity to flee into his city.
    Commentary

    While Krsna was turning his face away to avoid seeing a naked woman, Bana fled.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Gada, Kṛṣṇa’s younger brother, also had such powers, what to speak of Kṛṣṇa having those powers.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Kṛṣṇa appeared in the Yadu dynasty as the son of Vasudeva, before Gada, to manifest all his qualities (gadāgrajaḥ). Thus his actions were suitable.

    Analogy

    Bhagavān will not stare at what should not be stared at, even to win a battle. Kṛṣṇa turns His face and Bāṇa, his chariot gone and bow broken, slips back into his city. The Lord's modesty buys the demon one more breath — and that breath turns out to be the breath in which Śiva will plead for him.

    Important Words
    • jvaraḥ — fever
      Personified Śiva-jvara — a deity weapon, not a metaphor. Gauḍīyas read the verse's literalism as theology: even disease has a person; even fever serves a master. Bhagavān will return the favor in v. 23 by deploying His own Vaiṣṇava-jvara.
    • tri-śirāḥ tri-pāt — three-headed and three-footed
      Compound: tri (three) + śiras (head) / pāda (foot). Standard iconography of the Śiva-jvara — three heads for cold/heat/sweating, three feet for movement in all phases. The grotesque body marks the tāmasa quality of fever as Śiva-tattva's lesser servant.
    • abhyadhāvata — rushed toward
      Imperfect of abhi-√dhāv (to run at). The same direction-verb the asura used in v. 17 — running toward Bhagavān is what every Śiva-loyal force does in this chapter, and each one will end up taking shelter (v. 24).
    • diśaḥ daśa — the ten directions
      Eight cardinal/intercardinal + up + down. The cosmographic completeness of the Śiva-jvara's burn: he sets all space alight. Bhagavān's reply will not match scale but rank: one Vaiṣṇava-jvara sufficient against ten directions of Māheśvara-jvara.
    After Lord Śiva’s followers had been driven away, the Śiva-jvara, who had three heads and three feet, pressed forward to attack Lord Kṛṣṇa. As the Śiva-jvara approached, he seemed to burn everything in the ten directions.
    Purport

    Śrīla Viśvanātha Cakravartī quotes the following description of the Śiva-jvara: jvaras tri-padas tri-śirāḥ ṣaḍ-bhujo nava-locanaḥ bhasma-praharaṇo raudraḥ kālāntaka-yamopamaḥ “The terrible Śiva-jvara had three legs, three heads, six arms and nine eyes. Showering ashes, he resembled Yamarāja at the time of universal annihilation.”

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    After Lord Śiva's followers had been driven away, the Śiva-jvara, who had three heads and three feet, pressed forward to attack Lord Kṛṣṇa. As the Śiva-jvara approached, he seemed to burn everything in the ten directions.
    Commentary

    Jvara however ran towards him to fight. His form is described: he had three feet, three heads, six hands, nine eyes, and the ash weapon. Filled with anger he was like death personified at the time of annihilation.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Jvara rushed forward to fight (last phrase is understood but not stated in the text). Citsukha says that “Jvara fought” should be added to the verse. The bhūtas were driven away previously when Śiva fought. Or, because they fled, Jvara came. Hari-vaṁśa says: jvaras tri-padas tri-śirāḥ ṣaḍ-bhujo nava-locanaḥ bhasma-praharaṇo raudraḥ kālāntaka-yamopamaḥ nadan megha-sahasrasya tulya-nirghata-nisvanaḥ niḥśvasan jṛmbhanāṇs ca nidrān vitatanur bhṛśam The terrible Śiva-jvara had three legs, three heads, six arms and nine eyes. Showering ashes, he resembled Yamarāja at the time of universal annihilation. He breathed like a hurricane and roared like a thousand clouds. By yawning he spread sleep everywhere.

    Important Words
    • nārāyaṇaḥ devaḥ — Lord Nārāyaṇa
      The verse names Kṛṣṇa as Nārāyaṇa precisely at the moment of dispatching the Vaiṣṇava-jvara — the form-name and the weapon-name match. Gauḍīyas hear the equation: Nārāyaṇa-tattva is Kṛṣṇa-tattva acting through a Viṣṇu-mode.
    • vyasṛjat — He released
      Imperfect of vi-√sṛj (to send forth, emit). The same root as visarga (emission, creation). Bhagavān's deployment is creative, not destructive — He emits the Vaiṣṇava-jvara the way He emits worlds: as an expression of His will, not as effort.
    • vaiṣṇavaḥ — the Vaiṣṇava (jvara)
      The fever 'belonging to Viṣṇu'. Even Bhagavān's secondary weapons take the adjective vaiṣṇava — Gauḍīyas read this as a small but pointed proof that the highest theological adjective in Sanskrit takes Viṣṇu as its root, not Śiva or any other deity.
    • yuyudhāte jvarau ubhau — the two fevers fought
      Dual aorist of √yudh. The duel within the duel: the chapter's larger Kṛṣṇa-Śiva structure is mirrored at the fever level. Form mirrors form all the way down — the Bhāgavatam's standard fractal procedure.
    Seeing this personified weapon approach, Lord Nārāyaṇa then released His own personified fever weapon, the Viṣṇu-jvara. The Śiva-jvara and Viṣṇu-jvara thus battled each other.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Seeing this personified weapon approach, Lord Nārāyaṇa then released His own personified fever weapon, the Viṣṇu-jvara. The Śiva-jvara and Viṣṇu-jvara thus battled each other.
    Commentary

    Krsna created the cool fever weapon.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    There is also another slightly different version of the verse. Immediately (atha) Kṛṣṇa released his own weapon in a special manner (vi—sṛjān)—something more powerful than Śiva’s weapon. This was for play. The Lord is described as deva—he who plays, since he can even create the universe just by his will in the form of Nārāyaṇa.

    Important Words
    • alabdhvā abhayam anyatra — not finding fearlessness elsewhere
      Absolutive + accusative. The structural condition of true śaraṇāgati: only when every other shelter has been examined and rejected does the soul turn to Bhagavān. Gauḍīyas read this as the necessary preliminary to genuine prapatti.
    • śaraṇa-arthī — seeking shelter
      Compound: śaraṇa (shelter) + arthin (one seeking). The technical Gauḍīya term for the prapanna-jīva. Even a Śiva-weapon, on becoming śaraṇārthī of Kṛṣṇa, becomes momentarily a model for every bound soul.
    • hṛṣīkeśam — the master of the senses
      Compound: hṛṣīka (senses) + īśa (master). Kṛṣṇa as controller of the senses — Gītā 1.21 and onward. The address is chosen for the situation: the Śiva-jvara, a sensory-affliction-deity, surrenders to the lord of senses, the only one with jurisdiction.
    • prayata-añjaliḥ — with joined palms restrained
      Compound: prayata (self-controlled) + añjali (joined palms). The bodily posture of stuti. Gauḍīyas note: prayata is more than 'folded' — it implies inner saṁyama; añjali without prayata is just hand-folding.
    The Śiva-jvara, overwhelmed by the strength of the Viṣṇu-jvara, cried out in pain. But finding no refuge, the frightened Śiva-jvara approached Lord Kṛṣṇa, the master of the senses, hoping to attain His shelter. Thus with joined palms he began to praise the Lord.
    Purport

    As pointed out by Śrīla Viśvanātha Cakravartī, it is significant that the Śiva-jvara had to leave the side of his master, Lord Śiva, and directly take shelter of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Lord Kṛṣṇa.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    The Śiva-jvara, overwhelmed by the strength of the Viṣṇu-jvara, cried out in pain. But finding no refuge, the frightened Śiva-jvara approached Lord Kṛṣṇa, the master of the senses, hoping to attain His shelter. Thus with joined palms he began to praise the Lord.
    Commentary

    Jvara began to weep. Not finding relief from fear even after going to his own master Siva, knowing Siva could not protect him, being very afraid (bhita), he offered respects to Krsna on the ground, and with devotion he offered praise with folded hands.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Wailing loudly (samākrandan), the Śiva-jvara fought. Then he became afflicted by the strength of Viṣṇu-jvara. Not finding fearlessness elsewhere, wherever he went in fear, he was followed by Viṣṇu-jvara, like Durvasā being followed by Sudarśaṇa. He went everywhere in the mood of surrender, asking “Please protect me” but no one could save him from fear. Then, fearful, desiring protection or shelter (śaraṇārthī), he folded his hands, being purified by devotion, or enthusiastic with devotion (prayata) and praised the Lord. Another version has praṇata: bowing with devotion. Kṛṣṇa was master of his senses he thought compassionately of him. “Śiva-jvara, afflicted by me, is now surrendering to me.”

    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    Even Śiva's own weapon, when overwhelmed, runs not back to Śiva but forward to Kṛṣṇa. The Māheśvara-jvara discovers what every conditioned soul discovers — abhaya is found nowhere but in Bhagavān's hand. With joined palms the fever does what asuras rarely do: he begins to praise.

    Stories
    Gajendra's last refuge

    When the elephant Gajendra, gripped in the crocodile's jaws, exhausts his own strength and the strength of his herd, he finally calls out to Bhagavān (SB 8.2–3). The Lord arrives instantly because the call is finally addressed correctly.

    The Śiva-jvara's flight to Kṛṣṇa is the same gesture in a different body: defeated by a higher śakti, refuge is taken with the source of that śakti. Gauḍīyas treat Gajendra-mokṣa as the paradigm — and read this verse as its asura-side echo.

    Important Words
    • ananta-śaktim — of unlimited potencies
      Compound: ananta (unending) + śakti (potency). Gauḍīya theology centers on Bhagavān's śaktis (parā, aparā, jīva; svarūpa, taṭasthā, bahiraṅgā). The fever's first word names Bhagavān not as an attribute-set but as the locus of unlimited śakti — correct sambandha-jñāna in three syllables.
    • sarva-ātmānam — the Supersoul of all beings
      Compound: sarva (all) + ātman (self). Paramātmā-tattva — the second of the three realizations (Brahman, Paramātmā, Bhagavān). The Śiva-jvara correctly addresses Kṛṣṇa as the indwelling Self of all, not as one self among others.
    • jñapti-mātram — pure consciousness only
      Compound: jñapti (knowing) + mātra (only, sheer). Bhagavān is consciousness itself, not consciousness-possessing. Gauḍīyas distinguish this from Advaitin jñāna-mātra by holding that jñapti here is the svarūpa-jñāna of a Person, not impersonal awareness.
    • brahma-lingam — indirectly pointed to by the Vedas
      Compound: brahma + liṅga (sign, indicator). Gauḍīya commentators (Jīva in Bhāgavata-sandarbha) lean on this phrase: the Vedas point indirectly at Brahman, but the full Person Kṛṣṇa is the destination they point toward. Brahman is sign; Kṛṣṇa is the signified.
    • praśāntam — perfectly peaceful
      Past participle of pra-√śam. Bhagavān's śānti is not exhaustion-after-effort; it is svarūpa-śānti, peace as His native condition. The fever, agitation personified, names Kṛṣṇa by His opposite — the technique of stuti.
    The Śiva-jvara said: I bow down to You of unlimited potencies, the Supreme Lord, the Supersoul of all beings. You possess pure and complete consciousness and are the cause of cosmic creation, maintenance and dissolution. Perfectly peaceful, You are the Absolute Truth to whom the Vedas indirectly refer.
    Purport

    Previously the Śiva-jvara felt himself to be unlimitedly powerful and thus attempted to burn Śrī Kṛṣṇa. But now he himself has been burned, and understanding that Śrī Kṛṣṇa is the Supreme Lord, he humbly approaches to bow down and offer praise to the Absolute Truth. According to the ācāryas, the word sarvātmānam indicates that Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa is the Supersoul, the giver of consciousness to all living beings. Kṛṣṇa confirms this in the Bhagavad-gītā (15.15) : mattaḥ smṛtir jñānam apohanaṁ ca. “From Me come remembrance, knowledge and forgetfulness.” In his commentary Śrīla Viśvanātha Cakravartī emphasizes that the Śiva-jvara has realized in many ways Lord Kṛṣṇa’s supremacy over his own master, Lord Śiva. Thus the Śiva-jvara addresses Kṛṣṇa as ananta-śakti, “possessor of unlimited potency”; pareśa, “the supreme controller”; and sarvātmā, “the Supersoul of all beings” — even of Lord Śiva. The words kevalaṁ jñapti-mātram indicate that Lord Kṛṣṇa possesses pure omniscience. According to our limited understanding, we act in this world, but Lord Kṛṣṇa, with His unlimited understanding, performs infinite works of creation, maintenance and annihilation. As Śrīla Jīva Gosvāmī points out, even the functions of the gross elements, such as air, depend on Him. The Taittirīya Upaniṣad (2.8.1) confirms this: bhīṣāsmād vātaḥ-pavate. “Out of fear of Him, the wind blows.” Thus Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa is the ultimate object of worship for all living beings.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    The Śiva-jvara said: I bow down to You of unlimited potencies, the Supreme Lord, the Supersoul of all beings. You possess pure and complete consciousness and are the cause of cosmic creation, maintenance and dissolution. Perfectly peaceful, You are the Absolute Truth to whom the Vedas indirectly refer.
    Commentary

    You have unlimited powers. I have understood that your powers are greater than even those of Siva, my master. The reason is stated: he is the lord but you are the supreme lord (paresa). You are the paramatma of all beings (sarvatma) , even of lord Siva. You are pure spirit (kevalam jnati matram) without any mixture of material maya at any time. My master Siva has a mixture of maya. You are the creator, maintainer and destroyer, whereas my master Siva is only the destroyer. You are indicated by the Vedas (brahma lingam), whereas Siva is represented merely the sounds such as dentals and gutturals. (this statement about Siva actually is placed after the explanation of sarvatma but does not seem to make sense there.) You are the peaceful brahman whereas Siva is the ferocious brahman.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Even Śiva had begun to yawn because of Kṛṣṇa’s weapon. Understanding that Kṛṣṇa was the Supreme Lord, Śiva jvara then turned and approached him. He began praising Kṛṣṇa, indicating that he was worthy of surrender and worthy of praise and offered respects. Śrīdhara Svāmī explains that the Lord has unlimited śakti because he is the master of Brahmā and others. This is because he is the giver of consciousness of all beings (sarvātman). This is because he is pure consciousness alone (kevalaṁ jṣapti-mātram). He is the Supreme Lord because he gives consciousness to all others, and because he is also the creator of the universe. The meaning is this. Ātmā is pure consciousness and the giver of consciousness. From that consciousness arises inert prakṛti. That consciousness gives it power and that consciousness controls prakṛti. As the jīva in the material world, that consciousness takes up individual locations and as the Paramātmā it pervades everywhere. Therefore the five gross elements do not arise without you. Śruti says nāre bhīṣāsmād vātaḥ pavate: the wind out of fear of the Lord blows. (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.8) Eko devaḥ sarva-bhūteṣu gūḍhaḥ: the one lord resides deep within all beings. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad) The Lord has unlimited śaktis and is the controller of Brahmā and others. The Lord was defined in relation to the individual components of the universe. Then he is described in relation to the whole. He is the creator, maintainer and destroyer of the universe. (The Lord is Brahman as indicated by the Vedas.) He is without change or peaceful (praśāntam). Śrīdhara Svāmī says that because he is without change he cannot be directly described. The meaning is this. The products of change are perceived by everyone, since they arise from our realization. Scripture also can be understood directly. That which does not transform however, cannot be directly understood since it is different from what we normally experience. It can be somewhat suggested by scripture. “Brahman is without qualities. I however have qualities since I have a form.” Brahman is your form (liṅgam) which is revealed by that pure Brahman, which reveals your qualities, manifesting them through your svarūpa-śakti. Or you are described (liṅgam) by the Vedas (brahma). Or you have the characteristics of Brahman, realized by the wise since you are completely without change (pra--śāntam) or since you have a form of peaceful happiness.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    I bow to the one ātmā (kevalam) of all ātmās, present as Paramātmā in all hearts. You are the jīva-tattva (brahma) since they are your aṁśas and you are the aṁśī (non-difference of aṁśa and aṁśī). Moreover you are form of concentrated brahman (brahma-liṅgam) since you are parabrahman. Thus you’re the source of happiness (praśantam) or the very form of happiness.

The Śiva-jvara begins his stuti by naming Kṛṣṇa unlimited in śakti, Supreme Soul of all, pure consciousness, cause of creation-maintenance-dissolution — the very Tattva the Vedas indirectly point toward. The chapter's doctrinal heart begins here.

    Important Words
    • kālaḥ — time
      Time as Bhagavān's own form (Gītā 10.30 — kālaḥ kalayatām aham). Gauḍīyas read kāla as a śakti directly, not an independent reality; the Śiva-jvara correctly places it inside the māyā-list.
    • jīvaḥ — the living being
      The conditioned soul. Note where the verse places jīva: inside the list of māyā-effects, not outside. Gauḍīyas read this as the jīva's adhyāsa — he is mistakenly inside saṁsāra; bhakti is the procedure for stepping back out (acintya-bhedābheda).
    • bīja-roha-pravāhaḥ — the flow of seed and plant
      Compound: bīja (seed) + roha (sprouting) + pravāha (stream). The Bhāgavatam's signature image of saṁsāra's self-replication. Gauḍīyas cite this phrase in describing why karma alone cannot end karma — only Bhagavān, the negator (tat-niṣedham), can break the loop.
    • tat-niṣedham prapadye — I surrender to the negation of that
      Compound: tat (that) + niṣedha (negation) + prapadye (I take shelter). Prapadye is the technical Gauḍīya verb of śaraṇāgati (Gītā 18.66, BhP 11.5.41). The fever names Bhagavān as the very stopper of the cycle — not by absorption, but by sheltering the surrendered.
    Time; fate; karma; the jīva and his propensities; the subtle material elements; the material body; the life air; false ego; the various senses; and the totality of these as reflected in the living being’s subtle body — all this constitutes your material illusory energy, māyā, an endless cycle like that of seed and plant. I take shelter of You, the negation of this māyā.
    Purport

    The word bīja-roha-pravāha is explained as follows: The conditioned soul accepts a material body, with which he attempts to enjoy the material world. That body is the seed ( bīja ) of future material existence because when a person acts with that body he creates further reactions ( karma ), which grow ( roha ) into the obligation to accept another material body. In other words, material life is a chain of actions and reactions. The simple decision to surrender to the Supreme Lord releases the conditioned soul from this futile repetition of material growth and reaction. According to Śrīla Śrīdhara Svāmī, the words tan-niṣedhaṁ prapadye indicate that the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Lord Kṛṣṇa, is niṣedhāvadhi-bhūtam, “the limit of negation.” In other words, after all illusion is negated, the Absolute Truth remains. The process of education may be succinctly described as a way of eradicating ignorance through the attainment of knowledge. Through inductive, deductive and intuitive means, we attempt to refute the specious, the illusory and the imperfect and elevate ourselves to a platform of full knowledge. Ultimately, when all illusion is negated, that which remains firmly in place is the Absolute Truth, the Supreme Personality of Godhead. In the previous text, the Śiva-jvara described the Supreme Lord as sarvātmānaṁ kevalaṁ jñapti-mātram, “pure, concentrated spiritual consciousness.” Now the Śiva-jvara concludes his philosophical description of the Lord by saying in this text that the various aspects of material existence are also potencies of the Supreme Lord. Śrīla Viśvanātha Cakravartī mentions that the Supreme Lord’s own body and senses, as implied here by the word tan-niṣedham, are nondifferent from the Lord’s pure spiritual existence. The Lord’s body and senses are not external to Him, nor do they cover Him, but rather the Lord is identical with His spiritual form and senses. The full Absolute Truth, unlimited in fascinating diversity, is Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Time; fate; karma; the jīva and his propensities; the subtle material elements; the material body; the life air; false ego; the various senses; and the totality of these as reflected in the living being's subtle body—all this constitutes your material illusory energy, māyā, an endless cycle like that of seed and plant. I take shelter of You, the negation of this māyā.
    Commentary

    He begins to elaborate on the lord's pure consciousness (kevalam jnaptimatram). First the objects excluded by use of the word "only" (kevalam) are enumerated. Time (kala) is the agitator. Karma, action, is the subtle cause. That which brings about results is daiva. Svabhava is the ability to posess this daiva and karma. Jiva is the holder of this svabhava. Dravya refers to the subtle elements or tan matras. Ksetra is prakrti or matter. Prana is the sutra (math tattva??). Atma means ahankara. Vikara means the eleven senses. Mahabhutani are the five gross elements. The combination of the eleven senses and five gross elements is called the body. Acton generated from the body (bija) produces another body (roha). This continuous (pravaha) flow is your maya. Though the jiva is different from maya, because being controlled by maya it is enumerated with maya. I offer respects to the opposite of that maya. Your senses and body however are part of you, and are not maya.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    After offering respects, in order to surrender, he describes the Lord as the shelter of everything and uncontaminated by the faults of matter since he is pure consciousness etc. as described in the previous verse. After describing the Lord in this way, he surrenders. Kṣetram can mean prakṛti or the body. However taking the word to mean body would be repetitious. Jīva here refers to the jīva with upādhis. All of these are the play of your external energy (tvan-māyā). I take shelter of you since I am covered by māyā.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The list of elements is from most subtle to least subtle. Śrīdhara Svāmī explains the rest. I take shelter of you in order to achieve cessation of māyā by your mercy since I am included in the cycle of māyā. That is expressed in this verse. Daivam means that which takes the form of your wish. Svabhāva revers to peace etc. Kṣetra is the citta and intelligence. You cause the negation of this māyā. Thus you should forgive my sins, since I am overpowered by your māyā.

    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    A seed becomes a plant, the plant drops seeds, those seeds become plants — the cycle runs without an outside push. Saṁsāra is exactly this self-perpetuating crop. Kāla, karma, jīva, the senses, the subtle body — all of it, the Śiva-jvara confesses, is Your māyā, and I shelter in You as its negation.

    Important Words
    • līlayā — by pastime
      Instrumental of līlā. Bhagavān's actions are not exertion (yatna) but līlā — play. Gauḍīyas insist that even slaying demons is līlā for Kṛṣṇa; the same word covers Vraja's butter-stealing and Mathurā's wrestler-killing.
    • sādhūn — the saintly
      Accusative plural of sādhu. The technical Gauḍīya term for those whose conduct is shaped by bhakti — sat (truth) + suffix. Kṛṣṇa's avatāra protects sādhus; the same word fixes who counts as the protected class.
    • loka-setūn — the boundaries (bridges) of the worlds
      Compound: loka (world) + setu (bridge, embankment). Dharma maintains the embankments that prevent the worlds from flooding into each other. Bhagavān maintains setus the way an engineer maintains levees — for the lokas' habitability.
    • bhāra-hārāya bhūmeḥ — for removing the burden of the earth
      Compound: bhāra (burden) + hāra (remover) + bhūmi (earth). The standard Bhāgavata-Mahābhārata phrase explaining Kṛṣṇa's descent (SB 1.1.23, Bhīṣma at Mahābhārata Karṇa-parva). Gauḍīyas note: the earth's burden is asura-multiplication; Kṛṣṇa's cakra is its removal.
    With various intentions, You perform pastimes to maintain the demigods, the saintly persons and the codes of religion for this world. By these pastimes You also kill those who stray from the right path and live by violence. Indeed, your present incarnation is meant to relieve the earth’s burden.
    Purport

    As Lord Kṛṣṇa states in the Bhagavad-gītā (9.29) : samo ’haṁ sarva-bhūteṣu na me dveṣyo ’sti na priyaḥ ye bhajanti tu māṁ bhaktyā mayi te teṣu cāpy aham “I envy no one, nor am I partial to anyone. I am equal to all. But whoever renders service unto Me in devotion is a friend — is in Me — and I am also a friend to him.” The demigods and sages ( devān sādhūn ) are dedicated to executing the will of the Supreme Lord. The demigods act as cosmic administrators, and the sages, by their teachings and their good example, illumine the path of self-realization and holiness. But those who transgress the natural law, the law of God, and live by committing violence against others are vanquished by the Supreme Lord in His various pastime incarnations. As the Lord states in the Bhagavad-gītā (4.11) , ye yathā māṁ prapadyante tāṁs tathaiva bhajāmy aham. He is impartial, but He responds appropriately to the actions of the living beings.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    With various intentions, You perform pastimes to maintain the demigods, the saintly persons and the codes of religion for this world. By these pastimes You also kill those who stray from the right path and live by violence. Indeed, your present incarnation is meant to relieve the earth's burden.
    Commentary

    "If that is so, then why is there seen in me the material qualities of attachment and hatred revealed by my showing favor or punishment?" "You desire, ‘Let me protect the devotees who are favorable to me and kill the demons who are inimical to me.’ By accepting such intentions out of affection for your devotees, for your pastimes, you protect the devas such as Indra, the devotees and munis, who act as the shelter for the people of the world (loka setun), and you destroy those who wander from the path. Thus raga and dvesa, attachment and repulsion, being aspects of your affection for you devotee, are not maya. Thus I have understood that your birth is for relieving the burden of the earth, your own devotee."

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    “If I am without fault why do I sometimes kill?” By pastimes with your devotees which arise at the proper time, consisting of various goals such as protecting those who follow your devotees and killing those opposed to your devotees, you protect Indra and other devatās and the sages who are shelter for the general populace. You kill those who oppose the proper path since you are the avatāra who has appeared to relieve the earth of her burden since she is your great devotee. Because you are so merciful to your topmost devotees such as the earth, your violence against the wicked is your great quality, beyond māyā.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Though you previously gave mercy as Nārāyaṇa and various avatāras, now you have appeared to manifest you unlimited qualities as bhagavān to benefit the world. You support the devatās by pastimes and kill the deviants from the correct path, who cause violence to others. Or unmārgān refers to demons and wicked kings who violent the scriptural path and live by violence or off other’s lives, like Rākṣasas. You have appeared from Devakī (janma) to relieve the burden of the earth by giving mukti and bhakti as suitable to the person. Or now more the previously you are distributing mercy. You support the devatās by pastimes such as infant activities (nānā-bhāvaiḥ), accepted for playing, not like humans who are forced to accept bodies by karma. You perform your childhood actions to give the highest bliss to the devaṭas and others, not as the Lord complete in himself. You nourish those of proper conduct (sādhūn) and devotees (loka-setūn). You create fear (haṁsi) in the demons when they hear about you. They also begin to meditate on you. Or you take those following paths contrary to bhakti and by hearing etc. have them give up the wrong paths and take to the correct path. You take birth to decorate the earth. Since I am most sinful, save me, who have surrendered to you by your mercy at this time, though I should be killed.

    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    A king walks the city in disguise — feeding the loyal, lifting the saintly, watching over the borders, and quietly removing the bandits who live by violence. Kṛṣṇa's avatāra is exactly this circuit: He sustains devotees and dharmic boundaries; the slaying of demons is the same gesture, only the other side of it.

    Stories
    The avatāra-formula of Gītā 4.7-8

    Kṛṣṇa Himself states the principle in the Gītā: yadā yadā hi dharmasya glānir bhavati bhārata… paritrāṇāya sādhūnāṁ vināśāya ca duṣkṛtām, dharma-saṁsthāpanārthāya sambhavāmi yuge yuge.

    The Śiva-jvara is reciting this very theology back to Kṛṣṇa — maintaining devotees, killing those who live by hiṁsā, relieving the earth's burden. Gauḍīyas treat this verse and Gītā 4.7-8 as cross-references; the fever has correctly memorized the syllabus.
